questions.text: The silk routes linked which of the following regions in the pre-modern world?
options: Asia with Europe and northern Africa
questions.answer: (a) Asia with Europe and northern Africa — The silk routes were overland and maritime trade links connecting Asia with Europe and northern Africa; Chinese silk and pottery, Indian textiles and spices travelled along them.

questions.text: Ireland's great potato famine, which killed about a million people, occurred in the
questions.answer: (b) mid-1840s — Potato blight destroyed the crop in Ireland in the mid-1840s, causing widespread starvation and death.

questions.text: The Bretton Woods Conference of July 1944 was held in
questions.answer: (a) New Hampshire, USA — It was held at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, USA, and set up the IMF and the World Bank.

questions.text: The G-77 group of developing countries was formed to demand
questions.answer: (a) A New International Economic Order (NIEO) — They demanded a NIEO: real control over their natural resources, more development assistance, fairer prices for raw materials and better access to developed markets.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Rinderpest, a fast-spreading cattle disease, shook the lives and economies of Africa in the late nineteenth century.
Reason (R): The loss of cattle destroyed African livelihoods and made it easier for European colonisers to force Africans into the labour market.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.answer: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. — Rinderpest arrived in the late 1880s and killed about 90 per cent of the cattle; control over the scarce cattle helped the colonisers conquer Africans and force them to work for wages.

questions.text: The phase of industrialisation in Europe before the coming of factories, based on rural cottage production for an international market, is known as
questions.answer: (a) Proto-industrialisation — Peasants and artisans working at home for merchants for an international market is called proto-industrialisation.

questions.text: The spinning jenny, which speeded up the spinning process, was invented by
questions.answer: (a) James Hargreaves — James Hargreaves invented it in 1764. Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill.

questions.text: The steam engine designed by Thomas Newcomen was improved by
questions.answer: (a) James Watt — James Watt improved Newcomen's engine and patented it in 1781; his industrialist friend Matthew Boulton manufactured it.

questions.text: In the context of the East India Company's control over weavers in India, who were the gomasthas?
options: Paid servants appointed to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine the quality of cloth
Weavers who owned their own looms
questions.answer: (a) Paid servants appointed to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine the quality of cloth — The Company appointed paid servants called gomasthas for these tasks.

questions.text: Which of the following pairs of Indian port cities declined as the colonial trade expanded from the late eighteenth century?
questions.answer: (a) Surat and Hooghly — Old ports like Surat and Hooghly declined, while Bombay and Calcutta grew as new colonial ports.

questions.text: The first cotton mill in Bombay came up in
questions.answer: (a) 1854 — It was set up in 1854 and went into production two years later.

questions.text: By 1941, over 35 per cent of handlooms in India were fitted with
questions.answer: (a) Fly shuttles — The fly shuttle, a mechanical device for weaving, increased the productivity of weavers.

questions.text: In Indian mills, the person employed by industrialists to get new recruits and who helped them settle in the city was called a
questions.answer: (a) Jobber — The jobber was usually an old and trusted worker who got people from his village and helped them settle.

questions.text: The word 'bandanna', for a brightly coloured printed scarf, is derived from the Hindi word
questions.answer: (a) bandhna (to tie) — It comes from 'bandhna' (to tie), referring to cloth produced by a tying and dyeing method.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, merchants from towns in Europe began moving to the countryside.
Reason (R): In towns the powerful trade guilds controlled production and restricted the entry of new people into trade.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.answer: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. — Guilds regulated competition and prices and restricted entry, so merchants turned to peasants and artisans in the countryside.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Women who survived on hand spinning began attacking the new machines when the spinning jenny was introduced in the woollen industry in Britain.
Reason (R): The spinning jenny speeded up the spinning process and reduced the demand for labour.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.answer: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. — As the jenny reduced the demand for hand-spinners, women who depended on it feared losing their income.

questions.text: Rajasthan and Gujarat have enormous wind and solar energy resources which have not yet been developed properly. Such resources are called
questions.answer: (a) Potential resources — Potential resources are found in a region but have not been utilised so far.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Black soil is ideal for growing cotton.
Reason (R): Black soil is made of extremely fine clayey material, is rich in lime, iron, magnesium and potash, and has a high water-retaining capacity.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.answer: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. — Black (regur) soil develops from Deccan lava rocks, holds moisture and is rich in nutrients, so it suits cotton.

questions.text: According to the IUCN classification, species which are not found anywhere after searches of the areas where they may occur are called
questions.answer: (a) Extinct species — Extinct species are those not found after searches of known or likely areas, e.g. the Asiatic cheetah and the pink-headed duck.

questions.text: Which category of forest forms more than half of the total forest land of India?
questions.answer: (a) Reserved forests — More than half of the total forest land is reserved forest; almost one-third is protected forest.

questions.text: The Chipko movement was famous in the
questions.answer: (a) Himalayas — Villagers in the Himalayas hugged trees to protect them from felling.

questions.text: Project Tiger was launched in
questions.answer: (a) 1973 — Project Tiger was launched in 1973.

questions.text: Joint Forest Management (JFM) in India first started in the state of
questions.answer: (a) Odisha — JFM first started in Odisha in 1988, with local communities and the forest department jointly managing degraded forests.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a major cause of the decline of India's biodiversity?
questions.answer: (a) Habitat destruction — Habitat destruction by expanding agriculture, development projects, mining and overgrazing is a major cause.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Sacred groves help in the conservation of forests and wildlife in India.
Reason (R): Sacred groves are patches of forest left untouched by the local community and protected through religious beliefs, so many species survive there.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.answer: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. — No one is allowed to cut trees or harm animals in sacred groves, so they work as natural reserves.

questions.text: Which traditional system of rainwater harvesting uses underground tanks built within the house or courtyard in the semi-arid areas of Rajasthan?
questions.answer: (a) Tankas — In Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer, almost all houses traditionally had underground tanks (tankas) for drinking water.

questions.text: The Hirakud Dam has been built on the river
questions.answer: (a) Mahanadi — The Hirakud dam is on the Mahanadi in Odisha; Bhakra Nangal is on the Sutlej.

questions.text: Jawaharlal Nehru proclaimed dams as the 'temples of modern India' because
options: They integrate agricultural and industrial development and the economy of the nation
They were built by ancient kings
They were built only for drinking water
questions.answer: (a) They integrate agricultural and industrial development and the economy of the nation — He believed dams would integrate agricultural and industrial development and the village and urban economy.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): River valley projects are called multipurpose projects.
Reason (R): Dams serve irrigation, hydroelectric power, water supply, flood control, inland navigation and fish breeding.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.answer: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. — A multipurpose project serves several purposes at once, e.g. Bhakra Nangal, Hirakud, Damodar Valley.

questions.text: Which of the following is a rabi crop?
questions.answer: (a) Wheat — Rabi crops are sown in winter (October-December) and harvested in summer (April-June): wheat, barley, peas, gram, mustard.

questions.text: India is the largest producer of raw jute and jute goods and stands second as an exporter after
questions.answer: (a) Bangladesh — India is the largest producer of raw jute and jute goods and second as an exporter after Bangladesh.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): The Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) was set up at Sakchi (Jamshedpur).
Reason (R): The area had iron ore, coal and manganese nearby, water from the Subarnarekha and Kharkai rivers and easy access to Kolkata.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.answer: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. — TISCO was set up at Sakchi in 1907 because raw materials, water and a port/market were accessible.

questions.text: The Golden Quadrilateral Super Highways are being implemented by the
questions.answer: (a) National Highways Authority of India — The NHAI is implementing it.

questions.text: The Golden Quadrilateral connects which set of metropolitan cities?
questions.answer: (a) Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Mumbai — It links Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Mumbai by six-lane Super Highways.

questions.text: The North-South corridor links
questions.answer: (a) Srinagar and Kanyakumari — The North-South corridor connects Srinagar and Kanyakumari; the East-West corridor links Silchar and Porbandar.

questions.text: National Highways are constructed and maintained by the
questions.answer: (a) Central Public Works Department (CPWD) — CPWD maintains National Highways; State PWD maintains State Highways; Zila Parishad maintains district roads.

questions.text: Which of the following is the biggest port of India with a spacious natural and well-sheltered harbour?
questions.answer: (a) Mumbai — Mumbai is the biggest port, with a spacious natural and well-sheltered harbour.

questions.text: Which port was developed after Independence to relieve the pressure on the Mumbai port?
questions.answer: (a) Kandla — Kandla in Kuchchh, Gujarat, a tidal port, was the first port developed after Independence for this purpose.

questions.text: The pipeline connecting Salaya in Gujarat with Mathura in Uttar Pradesh carries
questions.answer: (a) Crude oil — The Salaya-Mathura pipeline carries crude oil; the HVJ pipeline carries natural gas.

questions.text: National Waterway No. 1 is located between
options: Prayagraj and Haldia on the Ganga
Sadiya and Dhubri on the Brahmaputra
Kottapuram and Kollam on the west coast
questions.answer: (a) Prayagraj and Haldia on the Ganga — NW-1 is on the Ganga between Prayagraj and Haldia (1,620 km).

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Roads are preferred for short distances while railways suit bulky goods over long distances.
Reason (R): Roads are flexible and give door-to-door service, and the cost of loading and unloading is low.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.answer: (b) Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A. — Both are true; door-to-door service explains the use of roads for short distances, but does not explain why railways suit long distances.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Air transport is the fastest mode of transport and is vital for reaching remote areas.
Reason (R): Air travel has made access easier to difficult terrain such as the mountains and the north-eastern states.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.answer: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. — Air travel is fastest and reaches inaccessible areas like the Himalayas and the north-east.

questions.text: Give any two reasons why the Great Depression began around 1929.
questions.answer: Any two: (i) Overproduction of agricultural goods, which led to a fall in agricultural prices. (ii) Falling prices and incomes pushed farmers to produce even more, worsening the glut. (iii) Many countries had financed investments through loans from the USA; when US lenders withdrew loans, these countries faced a crisis. (1 mark each)

questions.text: What is meant by a system of fixed exchange rates? How was it applied under the Bretton Woods system?
questions.answer: In a fixed exchange rate system national currencies are pegged to a standard at a fixed rate, i.e. rates do not fluctuate freely. (1) Under Bretton Woods, national currencies such as the Indian rupee were pegged to the US dollar at a fixed rate, while the dollar was in turn anchored to gold at 35 dollars per ounce. (1)

questions.text: Explain any two ways in which germs helped the Europeans in their conquest of the Americas.
questions.answer: (i) Native Americans had no immunity against diseases like smallpox that the Europeans carried from Europe. (1) (ii) Smallpox spread deep into the continent, killing and weakening whole communities even before any Europeans reached them, which made conquest easy. (1)

questions.text: Why did peasants and artisans in the countryside agree to work for merchants in the proto-industrial system? Give two reasons.
questions.answer: (i) Open fields were disappearing and commons were being enclosed, so cottagers and poor peasants who had depended on common lands for firewood, berries, vegetables, hay and straw needed other sources of income. (1) (ii) Their small plots could not provide work for all members of the family, so working for merchants gave additional income. (1)

questions.text: Who were a 'stapler' and a 'fuller' in the cloth trade of England?
questions.answer: A stapler is a person who 'staples' wool, i.e. sorts wool according to its fibre. (1) A fuller is a person who 'fulls' cloth, i.e. gathers it into pleats. (1)

questions.text: Mention any two ways in which the East India Company tried to establish control over weavers after its power was established in India.
questions.answer: (i) Appointed paid servants called gomasthas to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine the quality of cloth. (ii) Prevented Company weavers from dealing with other buyers. (iii) Gave advances (loans) to weavers, who then had to hand over the cloth they produced only to the gomastha. (1 mark each for any two)

questions.text: Why did industrialists in Victorian Britain prefer hand labour to machines in many industries? Give two reasons.
questions.answer: (i) There was no shortage of labour; poor peasants and vagrants moved to cities in large numbers, so wages were low and there was little incentive to use machines. (1) (ii) In seasonal industries (gas works, breweries, book binding, printing) demand fluctuated, so hand labour could be hired for the season only. (1)

questions.text: How did advertisements help in expanding the market for goods in the age of industrialisation? State any two ways.
questions.answer: (i) Advertisements made products appear desirable and necessary and shaped the minds of people, creating new consumers. (1) (ii) Manufacturers used labels, calendars, newspapers and magazines to make products familiar; labels with the 'Made in Manchester' mark and images of Indian gods and goddesses made the products acceptable to Indian buyers. (1)

questions.text: Distinguish between Bhangar and Khadar soils.
questions.answer: Bhangar is the older alluvium, with a higher concentration of kanker nodules, found away from the river on the upland. (1) Khadar is the newer alluvium, with finer particles and more fertile, found in flood plains and renewed almost every year. (1)

questions.text: What are endemic species? Give one example from India.
questions.answer: Endemic species are those found only in some particular areas, usually isolated by natural or geographical barriers. (1) Examples: Andaman wild pig, Nicobar pigeon, Mithun in Arunachal Pradesh. (1)

questions.text: Why is the conservation of forests and wildlife important? Give any two reasons.
questions.answer: (i) Conservation preserves ecological diversity and our life support systems: water, air and soil. (1) (ii) It preserves the genetic diversity of plants and animals, which is essential for agriculture and fisheries. (1)

questions.text: Name any two community-based efforts to conserve forests in India.
questions.answer: (i) Villagers of Sariska Tiger Reserve in Rajasthan fought against mining; villagers in Alwar protect the Bhairodev Dakav 'Sonchuri'. (ii) Chipko movement in the Himalayas; Beej Bachao Andolan in Tehri and Navdanya promoting crop diversity. (1 mark each for any two)

questions.text: Why is there water scarcity in India even though the country has large fresh water resources? Give two reasons.
questions.answer: (i) Over-exploitation and excessive use of water, unequal access to water among social groups, and a rapidly growing population needing more water. (1) (ii) Growth of industries and urbanisation, use of groundwater for irrigation (lowering the water table) and pollution of water by industrial and domestic wastes. (1)

questions.text: What are 'guls' or 'kuls'? Where are they used?
questions.answer: In the hilly and mountainous regions of the Western Himalayas, people built diversion channels called 'guls' or 'kuls' for agriculture. (1) They carry water from streams to fields, e.g. in Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir. (1)

questions.text: What was the Bhoodan-Gramdan Movement? Who started it?
questions.answer: Vinoba Bhave started the 'Bhoodan' movement, also called the Bloodless Revolution. (1) Landowners were asked to donate part of their land to landless farmers (Bhoodan); villages donated were called Gramdan. (1)

questions.text: Why is the iron and steel industry called a 'basic' industry? Give two reasons.
questions.answer: (i) It supplies raw material to other industries such as machine tools, construction and automobiles; it is the base for heavy, medium and light industries. (1) (ii) It is the basis of the industrial development of a nation; its products are used everywhere. (1)

questions.text: State any two advantages of roadways over railways.
questions.answer: (i) Construction cost of roads is much lower than that of railway lines. (ii) Roads can traverse more dissected and undulating topography and go up steep slopes of hills. (iii) Roads provide door-to-door service and cost of loading and unloading is lower. (iv) Roads act as feeders to other modes of transport. (1 mark each for any two)

questions.text: What are Border Roads? Mention their significance.
questions.answer: Border roads are roads of strategic importance built by the Border Roads Organisation (BRO), established in 1960, in the northern and north-eastern border areas. (1) They have improved accessibility in difficult terrain and remote border areas and help defence and development. (1)

questions.text: Why is pipeline transport considered useful? State two points.
questions.answer: (i) Pipelines transport crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas from oil fields to refineries, fertiliser factories and thermal power plants; solids can also be transported as slurry. (1) (ii) The initial cost of laying pipelines is high but subsequent running costs are minimal; it rules out transshipment losses and reduces load on road and rail. (1)

questions.text: Name any two exports and any two imports of India.
questions.answer: Exports: gems and jewellery, chemicals and related products, agro products, engineering goods. Imports: petroleum crude and products, pearls and precious stones, machinery, fertilisers. (1 mark for any two exports, 1 for any two imports)

questions.text: How did new technology help the nineteenth-century world economy? Explain with three examples.
questions.answer: Any three: (i) Railways moved goods and people faster and cheaper from the interior to the ports. (ii) Steamships replaced sailing ships and shortened travel time and cost. (iii) The telegraph speeded up the flow of information and orders. (iv) Refrigerated ships made it possible to carry perishable food such as meat over long distances, reducing meat prices in Europe. (1 mark each for any three)

questions.text: Who were indentured labourers? Describe their condition in the nineteenth century.
questions.answer: Indentured labourers were bonded labourers under a contract to work for an employer for a specific period, usually five years, in return for their passage to the new country. (1) Most Indian indentured workers came from eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, central India and dry districts of Tamil Nadu and were sent to the Caribbean islands (Trinidad, Guyana, Surinam), Mauritius and Fiji. (1) Many were recruited by agents on false promises about the work and the place of work; on the plantations living and working conditions were harsh and they had few legal rights. (1)

questions.text: Who was a jobber in Indian mills? Explain his role and how he came to exploit the workers.
questions.answer: Industrialists appointed jobbers to get new recruits. The jobber was an old and trusted worker who brought people from his village, ensured they got jobs, helped them settle in the city and gave them money in times of crisis. (1) In this way he became a person with authority and power. (1) Later he began to demand money and gifts for his favour and controlled the lives of the workers. (1)

questions.text: Describe the Indian textile trade before the arrival of European powers and how it changed after the 1750s.
questions.answer: (i) Before the age of machine industries, silk and cotton goods from India dominated the international market; fine textiles came from India. (1) (ii) The trade was carried by Armenian and Persian merchants over land routes through Afghanistan, Persia and Central Asia, and through sea ports such as Surat on the Gujarat coast, Masulipatam on the Coromandel coast and Hooghly in Bengal. (1) (iii) From the 1750s, as European companies gained power, the old network of Indian merchants broke down; Surat and Hooghly declined, while Bombay and Calcutta grew as new ports under European control. (1)

questions.text: Why did the market for Indian textiles collapse in the nineteenth century? Give three reasons.
questions.answer: (i) English cotton goods flooded the Indian market because the import duty on goods entering India was very low, while Indian cloth entering Britain faced high duties. (1) (ii) Exports of Indian cotton goods fell sharply. (1) (iii) From the 1860s, raw cotton exports from India to England increased, so Indian weavers faced a shortage of raw cotton at affordable prices; competition from cheap machine-made imports made weaving unprofitable and centres like Surat and Masulipatam declined. (1)

questions.text: How did the First World War benefit Indian industries? Explain.
questions.answer: (i) British mills were busy producing war supplies for the army, so Manchester imports into India declined. (1) (ii) Indian mills had a vast home market and were called upon to supply war needs: jute bags, cloth for army uniforms, tents, leather boots, horse and mule saddles and other items. (1) (iii) New factories were set up, old ones ran multiple shifts, many more workers were employed and everyone worked for longer hours; industrial production boomed. (1)

questions.text: Explain how labels and calendars were used by manufacturers to attract buyers in India.
questions.answer: (i) Manufacturers put labels on cloth bundles so that buyers could see the place of manufacture and the name of the company; the 'Made in Manchester' mark was a symbol of quality. (1) (ii) Labels and calendars carried images of Indian gods and goddesses, to make foreign goods appear acceptable and familiar to Indian buyers. (1) (iii) Calendars were used even by people who could not read and were hung in tea shops, homes and offices, so the product was seen day after day through the year. (1)

questions.text: Describe any three methods of soil conservation.
questions.answer: (i) Contour ploughing: ploughing along contour lines decelerates the flow of water down the slopes. (1) (ii) Terrace farming: steps are cut on slopes to restrict soil erosion; western and central Himalayas have well-developed terrace farming. (1) (iii) Strip cropping and shelter belts: strips of grass are left between crops to break the force of wind; rows of trees (shelter belts) protect coastal and dry regions and help stabilise sand dunes. (1)

questions.text: Explain any three ways in which local communities have helped in the conservation of forests and wildlife in India.
questions.answer: (i) In Sariska Tiger Reserve in Rajasthan, villagers fought against mining by citing the Wildlife Protection Act. (1) (ii) In Alwar district of Rajasthan, five villages declared 1,200 hectares of forest as the Bhairodev Dakav 'Sonchuri', with their own rules that do not allow hunting and protect wildlife against outside encroachment. (1) (iii) The Chipko movement in the Himalayas, the Beej Bachao Andolan in Tehri and Navdanya have shown that crop diversity can be conserved and chemical-based farming rejected. (1)

questions.text: Describe the main provisions of the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
questions.answer: (i) The Act was implemented with various provisions for protecting habitats and banning hunting. (1) (ii) It gave legal protection to the remaining populations of endangered species. (1) (iii) It provided for national parks and wildlife sanctuaries and for lists of protected species, with hunting prohibited. (1)

questions.text: Distinguish between reserved forests and protected forests.
questions.answer: (i) Reserved forests: more than half of the total forest land is reserved; they are regarded as the most valuable for the conservation of forest and wildlife resources. (1.5) (ii) Protected forests: almost one-third of the total forest area; they are protected from further depletion. (1.5)

questions.text: Write any three disadvantages of multipurpose river projects.
questions.answer: (i) Dams regulate or impound water flow, which restricts the natural flow of the river, causes excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir and poorer habitats for aquatic life. (1) (ii) Dams fragment rivers, making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate, especially for spawning; reservoirs submerge existing vegetation and soil. (1) (iii) Large-scale displacement of local communities, who lose land and livelihood, led to protests such as the Narmada Bachao Andolan and the Tehri Dam Andolan. (1)

questions.text: Explain how rainwater harvesting can help solve the water scarcity problem in India, with examples.
questions.answer: (i) Rainwater harvesting recharges groundwater and provides water for domestic and agricultural use. (1) (ii) Traditional methods: tankas in Rajasthan for drinking water; khadins and johads for agriculture; guls and kuls in the Western Himalayas. (1) (iii) Modern: rooftop rainwater harvesting in Gendathur village of Mysuru, Karnataka; Tamil Nadu made rooftop rainwater harvesting structures compulsory in all houses. (1)

questions.text: What institutional and technological reforms were made in Indian agriculture to improve the condition of farmers? Explain any three.
questions.answer: (i) Land reforms: collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, abolition of zamindari. (1) (ii) The Green Revolution and the White Revolution (Operation Flood) were the base of the agricultural development strategy. (1) (iii) Provision of crop insurance against drought, flood, cyclone, fire and disease; Grameen banks, cooperative societies and banks giving loans at low interest; Kisan Credit Card (KCC) and Personal Accident Insurance Scheme (PAIS). (1)

questions.text: Explain any three measures to control industrial pollution of water.
questions.answer: (i) Minimising the use of water for processing by reusing and recycling it in two or more successive stages. (1) (ii) Harvesting rainwater to meet water requirements. (1) (iii) Treating hot water and effluents before releasing them into rivers and ponds. (1)

questions.text: Explain the classification of roads in India.
questions.answer: (i) Golden Quadrilateral Super Highways and the North-South and East-West corridors, implemented by the NHAI. (1) (ii) National Highways link extreme parts of the country and are maintained by the CPWD; State Highways link state capitals with district headquarters and are maintained by State PWD; District roads are maintained by the Zila Parishad. (1) (iii) Other roads (rural roads) link villages, under the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana; Border Roads built by the BRO; and international roads linking India with neighbouring countries. (1)

questions.text: Explain the importance of railways in India. Write any three points.
questions.answer: (i) Railways are the principal mode of transportation for freight and passengers in India. (1) (ii) They conduct multifarious activities such as business, sightseeing and pilgrimage, and carry goods over long distances. (1) (iii) They carry bulky goods such as coal, iron ore and food grains and have played a major role in economic development and national integration; the Indian Railways is divided into 16 zones. (1)

questions.text: Describe any three major sea ports of India and their specialities.
questions.answer: Any three: (i) Mumbai: the biggest port, with a spacious natural and well-sheltered harbour. (ii) Kandla: a tidal port in Kuchchh developed after Independence to relieve pressure on Mumbai. (iii) Marmagao in Goa: the premier iron-ore exporting port. (iv) New Mangalore in Karnataka: exports iron ore from the Kudremukh mines. (v) Chennai: one of the oldest artificial ports. (vi) Visakhapatnam: the deepest landlocked and well-protected port. (vii) Kolkata: an inland riverine port on the Hugli. (1 mark each for any three)

questions.text: Explain the importance of tourism as a trade in India. Write any three points.
questions.answer: (i) Tourism has grown substantially over the last three decades and provides employment and foreign exchange. (1) (ii) It supports local handicrafts and cultural pursuits. (1) (iii) It promotes national integration and international understanding of India's culture and heritage; tourists visit for heritage, ecotourism, adventure, medical and business purposes. (1)

questions.text: Describe the impact of the Great Depression on the Indian economy.
questions.answer: (i) India's exports and imports nearly halved between 1928 and 1934. (1) (ii) As international prices crashed, prices in India also fell sharply; between 1928 and 1934 wheat prices in India fell by 50 per cent. (1) (iii) Peasants and farmers suffered more than urban people, since agricultural prices fell faster than prices of manufactured goods, while the colonial government refused to reduce the revenue demand. (1) (iv) Cultivators producing for the world market, such as the jute growers of Bengal, were badly hit and fell deeply into debt. (1) (v) Urban India was less affected; people with fixed incomes found that their real incomes rose as prices fell. India became an exporter of gold during the depression. (1)

questions.text: Explain the system of proto-industrialisation. Why did merchants find it profitable?
questions.answer: (i) Proto-industrialisation was the phase of industrial production, before the coming of factories, for an international market. (1) (ii) Merchants could not expand production in towns because urban crafts and trade guilds were powerful: they trained craftspeople, controlled production, regulated competition and prices and restricted the entry of new people into trade. (1) (iii) Merchants therefore moved to the countryside, supplying money to peasants and artisans to produce for the international market. (1) (iv) Poor peasants and cottagers, whose common lands were disappearing, agreed to work for merchants; the family earned additional income and worked at home. (1) (v) A clothier bought wool from a stapler and gave it to spinners; the thread went to weavers, fullers and dyers, and the cloth was taken to London for finishing before export. Merchants controlled this network of production. (1)

questions.text: Describe the impact of the East India Company's policies on the weavers of Bengal after 1760.
questions.answer: (i) The Company tried to eliminate existing traders and brokers who dealt with weavers and establish direct control over them; it appointed paid gomasthas to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine the quality of cloth. (1) (ii) It prevented Company weavers from dealing with other buyers, through the system of advances: weavers who took loans had to hand over the cloth they produced to the gomastha. (1) (iii) As loans flowed in and demand for fine cloth expanded, weavers eagerly took advances hoping to earn more; many peasant-weavers leased out their land and devoted all their time to weaving. (1) (iv) As the Company's power grew, gomasthas became arrogant outsiders with no long-term social link with the village; they marched into villages with sepoys and peons and punished weavers for delays in supply, often beating and flogging them. (1) (v) Weavers lost the power to bargain for better prices or to sell to other buyers; the price they received was miserably low and the loans kept them in debt. Many abandoned weaving, and in many places there were clashes between weavers and gomasthas. (1)

questions.text: 'Hand labour was often preferred to machines in Victorian Britain.' Examine the statement with reasons.
questions.answer: (i) There was no shortage of labour; poor peasants and vagrants moved to cities in large numbers in search of jobs, so wages were low. (1) (ii) Industrialists had no problem of labour shortage or high wage costs, so they had little incentive to introduce machines. (1) (iii) In seasonal industries such as gas works, breweries, book binding and printing, industrialists preferred hand labour, employing workers for the season only. (1) (iv) Where goods were required in a great variety of designs and shapes, human skill rather than mechanical technology was needed. (1) (v) The upper classes, aristocrats and the bourgeoisie, preferred things produced by hand; hand-made products symbolised refinement and class, being finished and carefully designed, while machine-made goods were meant for export and the working classes. (1)

questions.text: Classify resources on the basis of origin, exhaustibility and ownership, with an example for each category.
questions.answer: (i) Origin: biotic (obtained from the biosphere and having life, e.g. human beings, flora and fauna, livestock) and abiotic (non-living, e.g. rocks and metals). (1) (ii) Exhaustibility: renewable (can be renewed or reproduced, e.g. solar and wind energy, water, forests) and non-renewable (take very long geological time to form, e.g. minerals and fossil fuels). (2) (iii) Ownership: individual (e.g. plots, houses), community-owned (e.g. village commons, playgrounds, burial grounds), national (minerals, water, forests, wildlife and land within the political boundaries and oceanic area up to 12 nautical miles) and international (oceanic resources beyond 200 nautical miles of the Exclusive Economic Zone, regulated by international institutions). (2)

questions.text: Explain the steps taken by the Government of India to conserve forests and wildlife.
questions.answer: (i) The Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 provided for protecting habitats, banning hunting and giving legal protection to endangered species. (1) (ii) The central and state governments established national parks and wildlife sanctuaries and announced projects to protect gravely threatened animals, such as the tiger, one-horned rhinoceros, Asiatic lion, Kashmir stag and Indian elephant. (1) (iii) Project Tiger (1973) is one of the well-publicised wildlife campaigns in the world; tiger reserves were created. (1) (iv) Biosphere reserves were set up to protect wildlife, plants and the traditional lifestyle of communities. (1) (v) Joint Forest Management (starting in Odisha, 1988) involves local communities in the management and restoration of degraded forests. (1)

questions.text: 'Multipurpose projects promised to bring huge benefits.' Explain the benefits of dams and the reasons for opposition to them.
questions.answer: Benefits: (i) Dams serve irrigation, hydroelectric power generation, water supply for domestic and industrial uses, flood control, recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding. (1) (ii) Nehru called dams the 'temples of modern India' as they integrate agricultural and industrial development. (1) Opposition: (iii) Dams regulate river flow, causing excessive sedimentation and poor habitats for aquatic life. (1) (iv) Displacement of local communities led to movements like the Narmada Bachao Andolan and Tehri Dam Andolan. (1) (v) Dams meant to control floods have sometimes caused floods when reservoirs overflowed in heavy rain, and have caused loss of soil and vegetation. (1)

questions.text: Describe the three cropping seasons of India with examples of crops.
questions.answer: (i) Rabi: sown in winter from October to December and harvested in summer from April to June; crops: wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard; Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh are important wheat-growing states, helped by winter rain from western temperate cyclones. (2) (ii) Kharif: grown with the onset of the monsoon and harvested in September-October; crops: paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur, moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut and soyabean. (2) (iii) Zaid: a short season between rabi and kharif in the summer months; crops: watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder crops. (1)

questions.text: Describe the impact of industries on the environment and any measures to control it.
questions.answer: Impact: (i) Industries cause four types of pollution: air, water, land and noise. (1) (ii) Air pollution results from undesirable gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide from chemical and paper factories, brick kilns, refineries and smelting plants. (1) (iii) Water pollution from organic and inorganic industrial wastes discharged into rivers; thermal pollution from hot water; soil pollution from dumped wastes. (1) Measures: (iv) Reusing and recycling water, treating effluents before release. (1) (v) Fitting smoke stacks with electrostatic precipitators and scrubbers, using oil or gas instead of coal, and using generators and machinery that reduce noise. (1)

questions.text: Describe the role of transport and communication networks in the economic development of India.
questions.answer: (i) Transport carries goods and services from producers to consumers and connects sources of raw materials to factories and markets. (1) (ii) The pace of development of a country depends on the production of goods and services and their movement; roads, railways, pipelines, waterways and airways form a network. (1) (iii) Railways carry bulky goods and passengers over long distances, roads give door-to-door service, waterways are the cheapest for heavy goods, pipelines carry oil and gas, and air transport connects remote places. (1) (iv) Communication: personal communication (telephone, internet) and mass communication (radio, television, newspapers, films) share information quickly. (1) (v) Together they have made the world a global village and helped trade and tourism grow. (1)

questions.text: Compare roadways and railways as modes of transport in India.
questions.answer: Roadways: (i) cheaper to construct and can pass through undulating and hilly terrain; (ii) give door-to-door service and are flexible for short distances; (iii) act as feeders to railways, ports and airports. Railways: (iv) the principal mode for bulky goods and passengers over long distances; (v) conduct business, sightseeing and pilgrimage; the network is divided into 16 zones; (vi) less suited to hilly terrain than roads and require fixed tracks. (1 mark for each valid point, up to 5)

questions.text: Explain the significance of international trade for India. Why is it called an economic barometer?
questions.answer: (i) Trade is the exchange of goods among people, states and countries; international trade is trade between countries, and takes place through sea, air or land routes. (1) (ii) It makes available goods not produced at home. (1) (iii) It is called the economic barometer of a country, as the growth of trade is an index of its economic prosperity. (1) (iv) Exchange of surplus goods boosts production and economic strength. (1) (v) India exports gems and jewellery, chemicals, engineering goods and agro products, and imports petroleum, pearls and precious stones, machinery and fertilisers. (1)

questions.text:
Read the source and answer the questions that follow.
Food and the Corn Laws
After the Napoleonic Wars, prices of food in Britain increased as population grew and the demand for food rose. Under pressure from landed groups, the British government restricted the import of corn. The laws allowing the government to do this were commonly known as the Corn Laws. Unhappy with high food prices, industrialists and urban dwellers forced the abolition of the Corn Laws. After they were scrapped, food could be imported into Britain more cheaply than it could be produced within the country.
questions.answer: See subparts.

subparts.text: What were the Corn Laws?
subparts.answer: The laws under which the British government restricted the import of corn (food grains) into Britain.

subparts.text: Why did the landed groups want the import of corn to be restricted?
subparts.answer: Rising demand had raised food prices; restricting imports protected the high prices and profits of the domestic landowners.

subparts.text: Explain two consequences of the abolition of the Corn Laws for Britain.
subparts.answer: (i) Food could be imported more cheaply than it could be produced at home. (ii) British agriculture could not compete with imports; vast areas of land were left uncultivated and many people lost work and moved to cities or migrated overseas. (1 mark each)

questions.text:
Read the source and answer the questions that follow.
When Indian manufacturers advertised
By the late nineteenth century, manufacturers were printing images of Indian gods and goddesses on calendars and labels to make the products appear acceptable to the people. Calendars were used even by people who could not read, and they were hung in tea shops and in poor people's homes as much as in offices and middle-class apartments. Those who hung the calendars had to see the advertisements day after day through the year. Nationalist messages were also given: if you care for your nation, buy products that Indians produce. Advertisements became a vehicle of the nationalist message of swadeshi.
questions.answer: See subparts.

subparts.text: Why did manufacturers print images of Indian gods and goddesses on labels and calendars?
subparts.answer: To make the products appear acceptable and familiar, with divine approval, to Indian people.

subparts.text: Why were calendars an effective means of advertisement?
subparts.answer: They were used even by people who could not read and were hung in tea shops, homes and offices, so people saw the advertisement every day throughout the year.

subparts.text: How did advertisements become a vehicle of the nationalist message? Explain.
subparts.answer: Indian manufacturers gave nationalist messages in their advertisements, urging people to buy products made by Indians if they cared for the nation; this encouraged the swadeshi spirit and the use of Indian-made goods over imports. (2)

questions.text:
Read the source and answer the questions that follow.
The Himalayan Yew in trouble
The Himalayan Yew (Taxus wallichiana) is a medicinal plant found in parts of Arunachal Pradesh and Himachal Pradesh. A chemical compound called 'taxol' is extracted from its bark, needles, twigs and roots, and it has been successfully used to treat some cancers. It is the highest selling anti-cancer drug in the world. Over the last decade, thousands of yew trees have dried up in different parts of these states because the bark was stripped off in an unsustainable manner.
questions.answer: See subparts.

subparts.text: Name the chemical compound extracted from the Himalayan Yew.
subparts.answer: Taxol.

subparts.text: What is the compound used for?
subparts.answer: For treating some cancers; it is the highest selling anti-cancer drug in the world.

subparts.text: Why are the Himalayan Yew trees drying up? Suggest one measure to protect them.
subparts.answer: They are drying up because their bark and other parts are removed in an unsustainable way for extraction of taxol. (1) Measure: regulate extraction, cultivate the yew, involve local people in conservation. (1)

questions.text:
Read the source and answer the questions that follow.
Bamboo Drip Irrigation System
In Meghalaya, a 200-year-old system of tapping stream and spring water by using bamboo pipes is prevalent. About 18–20 litres of water entering the bamboo pipe system gets transported over several hundred metres and finally gets reduced to 20–80 drops per minute at the site of the plant. The flow of water into the pipes is controlled by manipulating the pipe positions.
questions.answer: See subparts.

subparts.text: Name the state where the bamboo drip irrigation system is practised.
subparts.answer: Meghalaya.

subparts.text: How many drops per minute does the water finally reduce to at the plant site?
subparts.answer: 20 to 80 drops per minute.

subparts.text: State one advantage of this method. Name one traditional method of rainwater harvesting from Rajasthan.
subparts.answer: Advantage: it uses local material, conserves water and needs no electricity. (1) Rajasthan: khadins, johads or tankas. (1)

questions.text:
Read the source and answer the questions that follow.
The Golden Quadrilateral and the corridors
The government has launched a major road development project linking Delhi-Kolkata-Chennai-Mumbai and Delhi by six-lane Super Highways. The North-South corridor linking Srinagar (Jammu and Kashmir) and Kanyakumari (Tamil Nadu), and the East-West corridor connecting Silchar (Assam) and Porbandar (Gujarat) are other components. The project is being implemented by the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI).
questions.answer: See subparts.

subparts.text: Which authority is implementing the Golden Quadrilateral Super Highways project?
subparts.answer: The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI).

subparts.text: Name the two end points of the East-West corridor.
subparts.answer: Silchar (Assam) and Porbandar (Gujarat).

subparts.text: Explain two benefits of the project for the economy.
subparts.answer: (i) Reduces the time and distance between major cities, improving the movement of goods and passengers. (ii) Promotes trade, industries and regional development along the highways. (1 mark each)

questions.text:
Read the source and answer the questions that follow.
Pipelines
Pipelines are used to transport crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas from oil fields to refineries, fertiliser factories and big thermal power plants. Solids can also be transported through a pipeline when converted into slurry. Oil India Limited (OIL) has pipelines from the Naharkatia oilfield in Upper Assam to Barauni in Bihar via Guwahati. The Salaya-Mathura pipeline connects Salaya in Gujarat to Mathura in Uttar Pradesh. The Hazira-Vijaipur-Jagdishpur (HVJ) gas pipeline connects Hazira in Gujarat with Jagdishpur in Uttar Pradesh.
questions.answer: See subparts.

subparts.text: Name the oil field from where the pipeline goes to Barauni.
subparts.answer: Naharkatia oilfield in Upper Assam.

subparts.text: What does the HVJ pipeline carry?
subparts.answer: Natural gas.

subparts.text: State two advantages of transporting by pipeline.
subparts.answer: (i) The initial cost of laying pipes is high but subsequent running costs are minimal. (ii) It rules out transshipment losses or delays and reduces the load on road and rail. (1 mark each)

questions.text:
Read the source and answer the questions that follow.
Ports
Oceans are the great highways of the world; ports are the gateways for sea-borne international trade. The overseas trade of India is mostly carried by sea. Kandla in Kuchchh was the first port developed soon after Independence to relieve the pressure on the Mumbai port. Marmagao in Goa is the premier iron-ore exporting port of the country, and Paradip in Odisha specialises in the export of iron ore.
questions.answer: See subparts.

subparts.text: Why was Kandla port developed after Independence?
subparts.answer: To reduce the pressure on the Mumbai port.

subparts.text: Which port is the premier iron-ore exporting port of India?
subparts.answer: Marmagao (Goa).

subparts.text: Why are ports described as gateways of international trade?
subparts.answer: Goods enter and leave a country through ports, which have loading and unloading facilities, warehousing and links to land transport; most of India's overseas trade is carried by sea. (2)
